newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU has discretion on state aid.
newsitem.headline: EU has discretion on state aid.

text.p: The European Commission's decision on Wednesday to allow 3.9 billion French francs ($766 million) in urgent aid to Credit Lyonnais has highlighted its role in monitoring government bail outs in the European Union.

The Commission often comes under pressure from national governments seeking to protect pet industries and companies and, like authorities elsewhere, is sometimes faced with the prospects of dealing with a company that is "too big to fail".

Credit Lyonnais, some Commission officials have said, is clearly a case of the latter. The rules, however, permit the Commission to refuse any further aid to the company, even if this means it goes under.
The Commission has, for example, been accused of letting Germany's largest shipbuilder, Bremer Vulkan, go bankrupt by insisting that it paid back subsidies.
But other struggling companies -- notably airlines -- have had huge salvage plans approved on the controversial condition that they do not ask for more.
The Commission's discretion comes courtesy of the EU treaty, which lays out the following rules:

- State aid that distorts competition by favouring certain industries or goods in trade between EU states is illegal throughout the 15-nation bloc because it is incompatible with the EU's single market.
- Some types of aid are specifically exempted from this, notably aid to make good damage caused by a natural disaster or "exceptional occurrences".
The latter phrasing is particularly open to interpretation. Some have argued that even a fall in currency values can be considered exceptional.
- Other types of aid are can be exempted at the Commission's discretion.

These include aid to promote development in abnormally poor regions, aid to remedy a serious disruption in a country's economy, and aid to help development of sectors or areas if the aid is not viewed as hurting the common interest.
Again, the latter allows for considerable interpretation.
When it comes to rescue plans, such as Credit Lyonnais's, the Commission often authorises the aid providing certain conditions are met.

These can include capacity cuts and divestments. Although it never formally demands that a company is privatised, it has encouraged this on a number of occasions, most notably with French computer firm Bull.
